title: Thermal and Timing Coupling
summary: Work through Thermal and Timing Coupling.

blocks.md: This lesson follows **Thermal and Timing Coupling** in *Workload Placement* (Vol IV).

blocks.source: Vol IV, Workload Placement, § Thermal and Timing Coupling
blocks.md: A permission core can suffer execution delays long after a heavy proposal workload has terminated, because thermal capacitance traps heat inside the package. While electrical droop and interconnect contention manifest over nanoseconds and microseconds, thermal coupling operates over seconds. When an accelerator and a real-time permission core share a silicon die, a cooling path, and an on-chip power management governor, sustained neural network inference can lower the clock frequency available to safety enforcement, and keep it lowered after the inference stops.

questions.q: The section **Thermal and Timing Coupling** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: The placement record binds the declared WCET and deadline to the execution domain, privilege, period, unloaded and loaded maxima, bus QoS, droop and thermal limits, mitigations, and the conditions left untested.
Privilege checks govern digital access while the shared rail powers the gates that perform them, so droop, clock faults, and shared resets are failure domains beneath privilege.
A refuted placement forces a remedy matched to the coupling (static reservation, spatial partitioning, separate silicon), each paid in a different currency and leaving a named residual.

Couplings act on different timescales (nanosecond droop, microsecond queueing, millisecond ticks, second-scale throttling, hour-scale chassis heat), which tells a rail-correlated fault from a temperature-correlated one.
